In 2025, India ran a goods deficit of well over $110 billion with China. Beijing is an important supplier of manufactured products, but it cannot offer India a market as big as that of the United States, nor can it provide India access to the range of advanced technology that the United States does. Russia likewise imports few Indian goods and is not a source of today’s advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence.
India’s recent trade diplomacy reflects its “America plus” strategy. Having refused to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2019, a group dominated by China, New Delhi has signed free trade agreements with New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the European Union. It has also expanded economic cooperation with Australia and renewed trade talks with Canada. The United States and India finalized a consequential trade deal in February, the first of its kind between the two countries, which promises to increase bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030. But Trump has yet to sign off on it and continues to look for new ways to impose tariffs on India.
India also relies on the United States and its partners for security. Tensions along the disputed Chinese-Indian border cooled after deadly clashes in 2020, but China remains India’s principal long-term adversary. The conventional military balance along the border favors Beijing. China spends four times more on defense than India does, has developed a massive military presence in the Tibet region across the Himalayas, continues to expand its naval presence in the Indian Ocean, and is deepening its defense relationship with Pakistan.
Washington provides New Delhi with access to intelligence, advanced military technology, joint exercises, and a wider network of security partnerships. The Quad continues to show potential as the regional maritime coalition that could limit Chinese domination of Asian waters. India has also expanded cooperation with U.S. allies on defense production, technology, resilient supply chains, and maritime security.
India couldn’t turn to China or Russia for these needs, even if it wanted to. India still relies on Russia for some weapons and spare parts, but Moscow’s capacity to balance China has diminished. Since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia is too reliant on China to be able to meaningfully curb Beijing. Nor can the BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, two groups dominated by China and backed by Russia, serve as sources of that balancing.
India understands that Washington has its own economic and political reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing. New Delhi is also convinced that the underlying competition between the United States and China—over technology, maritime power, alliances, and the regional order—will not disappear. Even if Trump softens Washington’s stance toward Beijing, the structural basis for U.S.-Indian cooperation is likely to endure.
Modi has so far managed to contain the damage caused by Trump. But there are limits to his capacity to do so. A growing section of India’s political class is itching to see New Delhi confront Washington, even if such a move hurts their country. The most immediate danger to the U.S.-Indian relationship comes from proposed U.S. legislation that would authorize tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian energy. If the bill becomes law—and Trump does not grant India a waiver—it would damage the Indian economy and contribute to a sense among Indians that the United States is no longer a natural partner. If the United States targets India while making allowances for other countries, a dormant anti-Americanism in India will reawaken.
Until recently, Modi’s domestic political dominance shielded his approach to the United States from domestic criticism. But recent youth protests, which began over leaked examination papers, have pierced Modi’s aura of invulnerability. If his authority at home continues to erode, he could face more backlash from both the right and the left over his perceived deference to Trump, and he may eventually find defying Washington to be politically useful.
Such anti-American sentiment may not produce a formal rupture in the relations with the United States. But it could slow defense and technological cooperation and provide more impetus to hedge. In the worst case, Modi might come under pressure to make concessions to China to stabilize the border and bring in more Chinese investment and technology. New Delhi would also have less reason to buy U.S. weapons. And India could stop playing a moderating role in the BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization—for example, by no longer diluting efforts to dethrone the U.S. dollar as the world’s dominant currency.
India has not yet reached that point. Critics of Modi’s prudent management of Washington have not come up with a convincing alternative strategy for how India should handle the growing power imbalance with China. It is easy to call for more productive ties with Beijing, but China’s terms for lasting peace with India—which include a territorial settlement that favors Beijing and reducing security ties with the United States—would be too costly to bear. Nor has China helped any other country rise economically or technologically. Put simply, India’s path to economic growth and technological modernization would be much harder without the United States. Strengthening ties with U.S. allies and working with Trump, for now, remains India’s best bet.
articles.summary: But Trump’s coercion could force Modi’s Hand.

articles.title: America Doesn’t Need More Nuclear Weapons
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ERIN D. DUMBACHER is Stanton Nuclear Security Senior Fellow and Director of the Defense and National Security Program at the Council on Foreign Relations.
How many nuclear weapons is enough? The question has haunted policymakers and scholars for 80 years. Early in the Cold War, the United States expanded its nuclear arsenal rapidly in response to the Soviet threat. But beginning in the 1980s, as the two nuclear powers sought ways to reduce nuclear risks, arms treaties helped cut the size of those arsenals significantly, and stockpiles decreased by 80 percent. Now, circumstances are pushing the United States to consider the size of its nuclear arsenal once again. Over the past six years, China has nearly tripled the number of nuclear weapons it has, and according to the U.S. Defense Department, the country is on track to have over 1,000 by 2030. China is not yet a nuclear peer to Russia and the United States, which each deploy roughly 1,550 nuclear weapons in keeping with the limit set by the 2010 New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, but parity may be Beijing’s goal. Meanwhile, the last formal barrier to a U.S.-Russian arms race fell away when New START expired earlier this year.
Faced with these rising dangers, the Trump administration announced in March that it would conduct what it called a “nuclear strategy review.” Some strategists recommend that the review include a call for a larger and more diverse nuclear arsenal. A larger arsenal, proponents of expansion argue, would provide the United States with a wider array of choices, especially for an in-kind response to low-yield theater nuclear attacks. Although Russia and the United States have nearly the same number of weapons, Russia possesses a greater number of theater nuclear weapons, which, unlike strategic nuclear forces, are designed for tactical use on the battlefield. China may also be developing more of these types of weapons. Advocates of expansion propose that if Washington can match any nuclear attack blow for blow, Beijing and Moscow will be less likely to initiate a nuclear exchange. According to Trump administration officials, the nuclear review will look at this “theater nuclear forces issue” to “identify where there may need to be changes or additions made.”
The United States should take additions to its nuclear forces off the table. The country already has a vast and diverse enough supply of nuclear weapons to unleash devastation on an adversary in the case of a nuclear attack. The purpose of nuclear deterrence is not to have an answer for every weapon in an adversary’s arsenal, but to avoid crossing the nuclear threshold in the first place. Moreover, introducing new theater weapons could provoke an arms race for which the United States is ill equipped and invite risks of inadvertent escalation that would only make the country more vulnerable. Rather than focus on expanding and diversifying the U.S. nuclear arsenal, Washington’s deterrence strategy should attend to the modernization of its existing strategic forces, which is behind schedule, and of its conventional arms, which are not fit to deter the United States’ greatest military threats, especially Chinese military aggression in the Western Pacific.
When the foundations of U.S. nuclear doctrine were laid early in the Cold War, escalation was understood as a ladder. When states encountered crises, their retaliatory actions would follow a vertical climb to more dangerous “rungs.” But escalation is unlikely to follow such a neat path, as Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby argued in May; instead, as he said, there are ways that nuclear powers can shape “the limits of a conflict” and influence how their opponents respond. The goal for modern U.S. nuclear doctrine, therefore, should not be an abstract conception of superiority at all levels of the escalation ladder but practical options to constrain and deter the adversary. The proposal to introduce new theater nuclear forces in Asia or Europe follows the outdated logic that escalation will progress in a rational, orderly way with increasing levels of violence and harm. It does not follow modern reality.
Without arms controls in place, Washington does need to modernize its strategic nuclear forces—high-yield weapons whose purpose is to hold valuable targets at risk—to deter and defend against a nuclear attack on the American homeland or on U.S. allies’ territory. It has been trying to do so for years, since the U.S. Senate ratified New START in 2010, but with mixed results. As part of a deal to gain Senate support for the treaty, U.S. President Barack Obama approved a multidecade program to upgrade the existing nuclear arsenal and delivery systems that is now costing at least $1 trillion. The decision paved the way for defense contractors and national laboratories to begin replacing bombers, ground-based intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarines, warheads, and military communications systems.
More than 15 years later, most of the United States’ nuclear modernization efforts are over budget and behind schedule, despite significant investments in workforce, infrastructure, and congressional appropriations that fulfill and sometimes exceed the funding the Pentagon has requested. In 2015, for example, Congress required that 80 plutonium components for nuclear weapons be built by 2030; Department of Energy officials have since deemed the task impossible. The Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile program was at least 81 percent over budget in 2024, and its first flight test has been delayed by about four years. The B-21 bomber program, which is on track, is the exception, not the rule. The United States is now at risk of nuclear disarmament by default. When the current systems reach end of life, replacements may not be ready. New work orders to build new weapons would only further stretch the nuclear enterprise’s capacity.
Expanding the U.S. arsenal would not only distract from modernization efforts. It would also invite new risks. A U.S. buildup would likely trigger a steady arms race with other nuclear states—the very outcome that Democratic and Republican administrations worked for decades to avoid through negotiations and mutual arms reduction agreements with Russia. And given the slow pace of the current nuclear modernization drive and the heavy burdens already falling on the U.S. defense industrial base, the United States today is not well positioned to win such a race.
The danger would not stop there. The greater the number and diversity of nuclear weapons, the greater the number of possible miscalculations and signaling problems in a crisis. For example, it would be difficult to distinguish between a nuclear-armed cruise missile that is launched from a fighter jet or submarine and a conventional missile. If the United States builds these capabilities, the Chinese and Russian militaries could mistakenly believe that an incoming conventional U.S. munition is nuclear. And because of the uncertainty, the risk of nuclear use would rise exponentially.
As long as no U.S. leader wants to fight a nuclear war, additional nuclear options, including more low-yield weapons, will be extraneous. Nuclear weapons are not effective for coercing an adversary during a conflict. If Washington responded to a nuclear attack with a nuclear weapon, whether that weapon was of similar yield or caused comparable damage, its opponent would not likely back down. Damage assessments would be hazy. Leaders would be likely to take on more, not less, risk, becoming more inclined to widen the war and respond with more nuclear attacks, including on U.S. territory. Deterrence requires that an adversary perceive both that a U.S. leader will use force and that an alternative course of action is preferable. A more diverse U.S. nuclear arsenal complicates any attempts to reassure the adversary that there is a better way out of a crisis. Ultimately, the potential benefits of expanding the U.S. nuclear arsenal do not justify the costs.
This is not to discount the rising nuclear threats from China and Russia. In 2018, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia would test dangerous new nuclear delivery systems that can loiter near the U.S. coast or maneuver at hypersonic speeds. China has built new silos in its western desert and has tested ballistic missiles in the Pacific. Neither U.S. nuclear weapons nor U.S. missile defense systems such as Golden Dome are likely to eliminate novel Russian systems or China’s nuclear expansion. Still, the United States’ 1,550 deployed bombs and warheads deter nuclear attacks from both China and Russia, provide counterstrike options to limit damage to the homeland if nuclear war does occur, and fulfill U.S. security commitments to allies and partners. Once China has nearly as many nuclear weapons as Russia and the United States, Washington may have new opportunities to pursue new arms control agreements with Beijing and Moscow.
The United States has long had good reason to place limits on its nuclear forces. In 1964, Defense Secretary Robert McNamara made the point that nuclear bombs would have diminishing returns once 400 strategic warheads—far fewer than Washington had at the time or has today—struck Soviet cities. Arms control agreements between Moscow and Washington since the 1970s have allowed the United States to avoid costly arms races. Dedicating funds to defense research and development enabled the U.S. military to achieve comparative advantages in conventional warfare capabilities, including advanced reconnaissance, combined arms, and precision strikes. Innovative conventional weapons still deliver options for U.S. presidents.
The Trump administration should similarly be thinking about nuclear weapons in the context of the United States’ broader military and deterrence strategy. Nuclear posture reviews have consistently affirmed, over the last four decades, that weapons in the U.S. arsenal are defensive, meant to deter aggression, and defeat peer adversaries if deterrence fails. In practice, the primary means of demonstrating the United States’ resolve to deny and defeat its rivals is conventional. The U.S. bombing of Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and Ukrainian drone strikes on military and industrial facilities deep within Russia over the last two years were conventional operations that achieved their tactical objectives. It would be sensible practice to include nuclear reviews as part of the national defense strategy process, as the last U.S. administration did. Isolating nuclear strategy from conventional force decisions is a mistake.
To be sure, conventional forces are not a substitute for nuclear weapons. But to credibly deter China and Russia, the United States needs nonnuclear options. The Trump administration has weakened U.S. conventional deterrence over the past year by pausing arms sales to Taiwan, shifting munitions to the Middle East, and beginning to withdraw American troops from Germany. Those steps must be reversed, and Washington must increase production of conventional forces capable of facing persistent threats in Asia and Europe, which includes both exquisite, or expensive and technologically advanced forces, as well as cheaper, mass-produced forces. U.S. policymakers should follow through on the promise of the third offset, an approach set out in 2014 for using unmanned and autonomous systems to counter Chinese and Russian military advances. With advanced conventional forces produced at scale, the United States can make the costs of war too high for China or Russia to initiate a conflict.
It is true that the global nuclear environment is changing. The United States must meet the prospect of two nuclear peers with foresight and planning. But the solution is not simply amassing more weapons. Building a larger and more diverse nuclear arsenal would put Washington on a path to undermining, rather than strengthening, deterrence. To counter both China and Russia, the United States must focus on modernizing its existing strategic nuclear capabilities and strengthening its conventional deterrence to preclude escalation. Because once a conflict transcends the nuclear threshold, no one can win.
articles.summary: Expanding the stockpile could weaken deterrence.

articles.title: The Future of Ukraine’s Drone Democracy
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
NATALIYA GUMENYUK is a Ukrainian journalist and CEO of Public Interest Journalist Lab. She is the author of the forthcoming book The Drone Revolution: How Ukrainians Changed the Way Wars Are Fought.
On August 19, the Ukrainian parliament voted overwhelmingly to confirm Ukraine’s new defense minister, ending weeks of uncertainty at a crucial phase of the war. For more than a month, Ukrainians had taken to the streets of Kyiv and other cities to protest President Volodymyr Zelensky’s firing of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. His successor, Yevhenii Khmara, is a special operations officer, best known for leading Operation Spider’s Web, the successful attack on Russian strategic bombers deep inside Russia.
But the political fallout from this summer’s upheaval is not over. The removal of Fedorov, whom many Ukrainians considered highly effective, set off a series of decisions by Zelensky to reshuffle the cabinet, and more consequentially, the heads of military and law enforcement agencies. Shortly after dismissing his defense minister, Zelensky sought to quell the public backlash by also firing Oleksandr Syrsky, the unpopular commander of the armed forces. As a result, the president was simultaneously replacing the two figures—the defense minister and the head of the military—officially responsible for Ukraine’s defense against Russia. That this was happening at the very moment Ukraine was gaining the advantage on the battlefield has made the changes all the more fraught.
For one thing, the large-scale protests themselves mark a new stage in Zelensky’s relationship to the electorate. Unlike any previous protests since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainians directly challenged the president’s handling of the war, introducing a dynamic that is unlikely to go away. Perhaps even more consequential, on the eve of the parliament’s vote on Fedorov’s successor, Fedorov released a controversial video address in which he declared that Ukraine needed a “system reboot” and called for wartime elections—the first time that not merely a prominent Ukrainian figure but a member of Zelensky’s inner circle and one of his former closest allies had done so. Until now, most Ukrainians have dismissed the prospect, since elections cannot be held while the country is under martial law.
Amid these developments, something else has become increasingly clear: one of the unforeseen consequences of Ukraine’s transition to drone-centered warfare has been the expansion of civil society in new ways. The embrace of a decentralized, technology-driven defense strategy has required new forms of cooperation between military and civilians, giving far more people a stake in matters of national security and military strategy. And that has created a new reality for the country’s leadership.
A crucial factor driving the events of this summer is the evolution of the military confrontation with Russia into a drone war. This reality, which began to take hold in 2024, has accelerated Ukraine’s transition from foreign-supplied to domestically produced weapons: some 95 percent of drones are now assembled inside the country. Moreover, although Ukraine remains heavily reliant on its scarce supply of American interceptors to defend against ballistic missile attacks, it is far less dependent on foreign systems and intelligence than it was at the start of the war. The shift to a drone-centered battle space has fundamentally altered combat tactics, the expertise required of soldiers, and the way arms are purchased. It has also rendered some kinds of legacy systems, such as armored vehicles and short-range artillery, increasingly obsolete.
Yet it is not the drones themselves that have made the shift so dramatic. To exploit the full potential of unmanned warfare, Ukraine has adopted an integrated digital architecture linking unmanned platforms with situational inputs and intelligence. It has also pursued an unprecedented level of digital coordination, as well as decentralized production and procurement of weapons and of digital technologies themselves. Fedorov was one of the key architects behind the deployment of this drone infrastructure. Unlike many other officials or military leaders, he not only possessed an acute understanding of the battlefield, the weapons deployed in it, and the data streaming from it, but he also had the ability to build, coordinate, and continually upgrade a comprehensive digital system to manage it.
Although he served as defense minister for only six months, Fedorov had driven this shift as the head of the Ministry of Digital Transformation, a government agency he created in 2019 and ran until 2026. Drawing on a team of specialists, the agency had set out to replace traditional bureaucratic procedures across government with more efficient digital platforms; a secondary goal was reducing corruption. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedorov’s team became a driving force within the government for Ukraine’s drone program. Since the acquisition of drones initially fell outside formal procurement, the agency was able to largely run the process through its own “Drone Line” initiative. At the same time, it began building a new digital infrastructure to manage drone warfare.
Some of these capabilities, such as Delta—a cloud-based system for managing the entire battlefield—had been designed earlier by volunteer-led civic initiatives. But the Ministry of Digital Transformation gave them crucial government support. It also introduced rewards for army units that successfully deployed drones and, later, for those operating unmanned maritime systems and ground robots, as well. Some military analysts worry that these kinds of incentives risk “gamifying” the war or that they oversimplify operational realities. Yet by providing continuous feedback, the programs provide valuable real-time battlefield intelligence, as well as sophisticated data sets for assessing the performance of weapons and units.
Fedorov’s team, relying for a time on Zelensky’s backing, pushed for new policies and funding mechanisms to accelerate the military’s digital transformation. It also set out to streamline the military bureaucracy and bring greater transparency to wartime procurement, which has been highly vulnerable to corruption. Over 900 Ukrainian companies now produce thousands of drone models and components. To manage this huge and fragmented sector, the ministry introduced new systems to coordinate logistics, certification, and deployment.
Overall, these changes have been significant. Step by step, drones have allowed Ukraine’s armed forces to acquire or sustain capabilities that have traditionally come from missiles and airpower. In 2025, Ukraine had reached parity in the air domain with Russia along the frontline; by 2026, Ukrainian drones and missiles were also able to reach Russian command-and-control centers, cut off logistics, and prevent some Russian assaults. Although Moscow can still outcompete on resources, using oil revenues and vast state spending to finance its aggression, Ukraine’s new digital architecture has enabled it to do more with less, multiplying the effect of particular weapons by connecting sensors, operators, and strike platforms into a unified system.
Despite their undeniable value, these innovations have often come from outside Ukraine’s military establishment, and sometimes in opposition to it. Overshadowed by the large number of civilian recruits after 2022 is the fact that the Ukrainian army began the war staffed by professional soldiers, with inherited doctrines and lines of command. Although the military established the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch in 2024, its traditional mechanized, infantry, and armored brigades still bore the brunt of the fighting while integrating drones at their own pace. And as with any large national armed forces, the existing hierarchy has resisted wholesale change. Many commanders have embraced drones as weapons—just as they would tanks or guns—yet without fully understanding the structural changes needed to make them effective.
Similarly, Ukraine’s established defense industry, which has long counted on existing relationships and contracts, has also resisted the overhaul. Until recently, drone contracting has remained a comparatively small sector. Even though it involves hundreds of millions of dollars, expensive traditional capabilities such as artillery and other conventional weapons systems continue to consume most of Ukraine’s defense budget. Over the past year, however, the balance has shifted: the military’s procurement priorities and the financial interests surrounding them have begun to adjust to drone-centered warfare. And that has created new forms of pushback.
Almost from the beginning of his tenure as defense minister, Fedorov and his team were targeted by smear campaigns on anonymous Telegram channels. These have linked him to various military scandals and alleged corruption in the drone industry. Fedorov blames the attacks on entrenched interests—defense contractors and powerful insiders—who were threatened by the shift in war priorities. As one example, he has cited his successful efforts to reduce the price of a procurement deal for short-range artillery that was becoming obsolete, given the expanding kill zones. He also said that Zelensky had received persistent complaints that the digital reformers were breaking a functioning system and disrupting the delivery of essential equipment to frontline troops.
At the same time, as large amounts of funding, especially from Ukraine’s international partners, have been directed at drone technology, established defense contractors and well-connected political actors have sought to gain a piece of the pie. They are now moving aggressively to compete with drone startups on drone contracts. Taken together, these tensions brought pressure on Zelensky to move more slowly on the military transformation—which Fedorov had been pushing to accelerate. But the president had failed to understand just how much the public had become invested in Ukraine’s new way of war, and the remarkable results it had begun to achieve.
By the spring of 2026, if defense contractors had misgivings about Fedorov, the Ukrainian public had become increasingly dissatisfied with Syrsky, Ukraine’s commander in chief. Syrsky had notched several strategic victories, including the battle for Kyiv and the liberation of the Kharkiv region during the first year of the all-out war. He had also embraced drone warfare, expanding drone procurement and battlefield integration, although that was part of the army’s broader evolution. Yet many soldiers saw him as a commander who emphasized discipline and was prepared to sacrifice lives when he considered it necessary to achieve a military objective.
Within the military, Syrsky had long taken pride in staying close to the frontlines, sometimes to the point of micromanaging the battlefield. But there was also a growing sense among officers and soldiers that he was beginning to value personal loyalty within the command structure above military effectiveness. He had a tendency to sideline talented younger officers and to use his control over promotions and resources to consolidate his own influence. According to some soldiers and officers, these habits risked undermining battlefield readiness, including on the most critical sectors of the front.
Then, in June, Ukrainian journalists published a bombshell investigation uncovering horrific allegations of abuse in an assault regiment—a unit that had been given privileged support by Syrsky. The revelations included evidence of violence and unlawful killings within the unit. Although a formal military investigation followed, public criticism remained intense and serving military personnel spoke out. Many laid the blame on Syrsky personally for allowing this to happen.
It was after this scandal that Zelensky made the ill-timed decision to fire Fedorov. In the eyes of many Ukrainians, the president was siding with those who opposed reforms. Almost immediately, thousands of people took to the streets of Kyiv and other cities. To contain the public outcry, Zelensky then moved quickly to fire Syrsky and install Major General Mykhailo Drapatyi as his replacement, a choice that was broadly welcomed. Drapatyi, 43, had entered the military in 2014 as a battalion commander and risen through the ranks, while taking part in many defining battles. He is known for embracing new approaches, including the digital battlefield promoted by Fedorov, supporting promising officers, challenging army leaders when necessary, and championing operations that minimize casualties—a priority that Ukrainians value.
Meanwhile, Zelensky named Khmara to replace Fedorov. Since 2011, Khmara—in his late 30s or early 40s—had served in Alpha, the Security Service of Ukraine’s special forces unit, and was considered to have an unblemished record. (He had to leave active military service and formally become a civilian before assuming the post, which by law must be held by a civilian.) Yet Zelensky’s moves failed to resolve the underlying tension between the Defense Ministry and the military’s general staff. By law, the defense minister is supposed to nominate the commander in chief to the president. But this time, Zelensky once again effectively selected the commander himself, creating a situation in which the general staff continues to see that it answers to the president, not to the defense minister.
A larger question is how this political upheaval will affect the war. Fedorov was fired just as the reforms he had been advocating for were helping Ukraine turn the tide against Russia. By spring 2026, Ukrainian long-range drone strikes were beginning to erode one of Russia’s greatest strategic advantages: its oil sector. Kyiv also continued to disrupt Russian logistics in the south, particularly in Crimea, while also attacking oil refineries across the European part of Russia, including Moscow and St. Petersburg. But many wonder whether Fedorov’s dismissal will slow that progress.
In Russia, pro-war commentators openly celebrated Zelensky’s decision, viewing it as a rejection of one of the main architects of Ukraine’s military modernization. Hours after his dismissal, representatives of several foreign governments and international technology firms, including the Italian minister of defense and Palantir’s CEO, Alex Karp, offered him positions, which he declined. Zelensky has also offered him several alternative roles in Kyiv, but Fedorov has refused them all because they came with limited decision-making power. Still, he seems almost certain to gain an important place within the government or defense sector sooner or later.
Despite Zelensky’s appointment of innovation-minded leaders to replace Fedorov and Syrsky, the future of Ukraine’s digital war ecosystem remains uncertain. Unlike Khmara, who takes office without an established cadre, Fedorov brought to the defense ministry the team he had already built at the Ministry of Digital Transformation. Although only a few of the digitization specialists Fedorov brought to the Defense Ministry have left so far, many more may be pushed out. By calling for elections, Fedorov signaled a move into opposition, raising questions about whether his relationship with Zelensky would deteriorate—and what this would mean for close associates still holding official posts.
By design, Ukraine’s digital battlefield infrastructure has the capacity to rapidly evolve in response to changing combat demands. The system can function without Fedorov or his team, but it remains unclear whether it can maintain the pace of evolution needed to stay ahead of Russia. The immediate risk is lost momentum.
The democratic culture that took hold in Ukraine in 2014 and drove the protests this summer continues to be one of the country’s greatest military strengths. Many of Ukraine’s most important military adaptations have come from below—from individual soldiers and commanders but also from civilian entrepreneurs. Hundreds of private initiatives have advanced technologies, software, manufacturing, and logistics in ways that have dramatically improved the way Ukraine fights. Too many military units, entrepreneurs, engineers, and civic activists are now invested in this ecosystem for a single political decision to dismantle it. But the disruption could affect Ukraine’s ability to iterate new advances on the battlefield—at a moment when the overall dynamic of the war hangs in the balance.
For Zelensky, the political damage of his decisions this summer cannot be undone. Ukrainians have largely remained united behind the president in the face of external pressure, including after Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. Nonetheless, he has shown more than once that he is out of step with ordinary Ukrainians. Already a year ago, his effort to restrict the role of Ukraine’s anticorruption authorities provoked major protests and significantly diminished confidence in his leadership. Now, his decision to fire Fedorov has only reinforced that perception.
Until this summer, Fedorov had avoided attention, presenting himself as a manager, not a politician. Yet Zelensky’s abrupt decision to dismiss him—for reasons the public still does not understand—made Fedorov one of Ukraine’s most popular figures almost overnight. Now, Fedorov’s call for elections has significantly raised the stakes. In his video address, Fedorov—without mentioning names—again spoke about powerful vested interests that have meddled in government and defense and resisted the changes Ukraine needs to maintain its military advantage. He also asserted that, with no end to the war in sight, Ukraine needs a broader debate about political accountability and decision-making. Clarifying his initially vague but surprising address, the former minister pledged to outline the technical and security logistics of wartime voting—specifically for soldiers, refugees, and frontline residents—to enable a realistic debate on holding elections.
Under martial law, elections are barred. Until now, only external powers—Russia or the United States—had questioned Ukraine’s political legitimacy without elections. Most Ukrainians deemed wartime voting dangerous and impractical, fearing that staging elections would simply divert attention, funds, and effort from the front. But Zelensky is in his seventh year as president, under a constitution that permits two consecutive five-year terms. Having made consequential, unpopular decisions, he has increasingly given the sense that he has stopped reading the country’s mood. Fedorov’s announcement may not precipitate an immediate change, but it has started a debate that could play out in the coming months and years.
Until now, when it came to the question of holding elections, it had seemed that Ukraine would know when the moment arrived: at some point, in an active, outspoken society, even during war, Ukrainians themselves would demand democratic accountability. This does not mean that Fedorov will automatically gain popularity if he decides to run. His call for wartime voting has alienated some public figures and politicians who backed him as defense minister. They see his intervention now as less a push for accountability than an open political challenge to Zelensky—one that risks draining attention from the reforms that Fedorov had previously championed. With the war likely to continue for the foreseeable future, the urgent question facing the country now is to what degree the people should be given a direct say in the war’s course: how it fights, by what means, according to what strategy, and with what broader vision for its defense.
articles.summary: Transforming the military has changed the war—and upended politics.

articles.title: The New Right’s Grand Strategy After Trump
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
LEONARD A. SCHUETTE is a Fellow in the Europe Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He was an International Security Program Fellow at the Belfer Center at the Harvard Kennedy School from 2025 to 2026.
The debate about American grand strategy has long been shaped by familiar schools of thought: restraint, liberal internationalism, and primacy. But the intellectual movement that provided the ideological fuel for U.S. President Donald Trump’s rise to power, the New Right, is forging a new contender: call it “civilizationism.” References to Western civilization permeate strategy documents and speeches by key members of the administration. Vice President JD Vance set the tone in his February 2025 speech at the Munich Security Conference, stressing the “threat from within” to the fundamental values that characterize “our shared civilization.” The Trump administration’s National Security Strategy warned of “civilizational erasure.” This January, at Davos, Trump emphasized “the bonds we share with Europe as a civilization”; the next month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on the United States’ transatlantic partners to “renew the greatest civilization in human history.”
The notion that there is a Western civilization and that it is superior is, of course, not new. But the concept of the West espoused by the New Right—and how that concept ought to guide U.S. grand strategy—is fundamentally different from how most had previously understood it. It is not based on a creedal understanding of Western identity as rooted in a shared set of principles that anyone, regardless of origin, can espouse, such as constitutional democracy, liberty, and equality. Instead, for thinkers on the New Right, the West is defined by a specific geographic territory, a shared ancestry, and Christianity.
Extended to the realm of foreign policy, this reimagination of the foundations of Western civilization demands a new and distinct grand strategy. Civilizationism is still a work in progress. Writings on foreign policy by New Right thinkers are limited, and the camp is internally divided. But by examining those texts and following the movement’s domestic ideas to their logical conclusion, it is possible to discern a distinct worldview. Civilizationists would aim to structure the world along bounded civilizational spaces, each dominated by a hegemon. They believe the United States is rightfully the hegemon of the West, dedicated to defending the civilization’s borders, urging Europe to uphold purported Western values, and pursuing coexistence with other civilizations, such as the Chinese, rather than aspiring to global leadership. They reject the universal ambitions of primacy and the constraints imposed on U.S. sovereignty by liberal internationalism. Civilizationism also differs from restraint, requiring dominance over the Western Hemisphere, by military intervention if necessary. And unlike realist visions that justify a great power’s control over its backyard by pointing to its legitimate security interests, civilizationism offers an ideological justification for spheres of influence and their boundaries.
Despite the Trump administration’s embrace of civilizational rhetoric, in practice its foreign policy diverges from what civilizationism would advocate and many of Trump’s own backers hoped he would pursue. Even if Republicans win the White House again in 2028, that would not mean civilizationism will become U.S. grand strategy; the New Right would also have to prevail over the party’s establishment faction. But at least two factors seem to favor the New Right in the intraparty battle. One is demographic: most polling shows a generational divide among Republicans, with younger voters more supportive of positions such as scaling back the U.S. role in the Middle East and retreating from viewing China as a major threat. The other is Trump’s war on Iran. As the consequences of this strategically catastrophic campaign become ever more apparent, the New Right’s clout is set to grow, having opposed the war from the start.
For decades, Washington’s foreign policy establishment advocated for different varieties of liberal hegemony. Even during Trump’s first term, traditional foreign policy elites exercised great influence and maintained relative policy continuity abroad. But Trump’s second term has fundamentally disrupted the intellectual consensus that long governed foreign policy debates, bringing the New Right into the discussions that shape U.S. strategy. This movement is composed of various factions, as Laura Field has distilled in her authoritative work Furious Minds. The postliberals want to enforce a Catholic conception of the common good and morality. Idolizing the American founding, the Claremonters propose radical, counterrevolutionary action to restore government by consent, shatter the administrative state, and cultivate civic virtue. The national conservatives embrace Christian nationalism and seek to bulwark the homogeneous nation-state from threats from liberalism.
What unites these disparate camps is a rejection of core tenets of traditional conservatism, such as limited government, neoliberal economics, and hawkish foreign policy, and a shared opposition to the creedal concept of American identity. Instead, the New Right views American identity in ethnoreligious and collective terms and considers the United States to be a fundamentally white, Christian, homogeneous country whose origins lie in European civilization. Its adherents believe that the relentless pursuit of maximizing individual freedom and rights has come at the cost of community, religion, and traditional norms. In other words, the movement sees liberalism not as the foundation but as the cancer of Western civilization.
The New Right has now drawn unprecedentedly close to power, having perceived the ascent of a self-advertised disruptor president—Trump—as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and seized it. In Vance, the movement has a prominent and influential figurehead, flanked by leaders such as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, Missouri Senator Josh Hawley, and the media personality Tucker Carlson. It is institutionalizing its influence in the conservative intellectual ecosystem. Formerly peripheral institutions such as the Claremont Institute; the once establishment, now Trumpist Heritage Foundation; and new entrants such as the America First Policy Institute, the Center for Renewing America, and American Moment currently drive debates on the right on issues as varied as trade and foreign policy. These organizations have trained swaths of Trump political appointees: by one count, at least 70 alumni of Claremont fellowships, including the director of the White House Office of Management and Budget and the deputy national security adviser, serve in the current administration.
The New Right’s vision of the United States translates into a distinctive foreign policy that seeks to strengthen the illiberal foundation of American society and protect its version of Western civilizational heritage. Civilizations, at least in the crude understanding popularized by the late political scientist Samuel Huntington, are homogeneous cultural entities defined by inherited traits such as religion, history, and language. Huntington maintained that the distinctions between civilizations were more fundamental and immutable than mere differences in political ideologies: they were “the product of centuries.” He predicted that as power dispersed among civilizations, their cultural differences would become irresolvable and generate conflict, especially as the West’s dominance and universalist ambitions became ever more contested.
The New Right’s logic of civilizationism, however, is more Schmittian than Huntingtonian. Carl Schmitt, the Nazi jurist known for his work on the friend-enemy distinction, is widely read among New Right thinkers; he also developed an argument on how to structure the international order. Schmitt proposed that the world would be properly organized by spatial blocs, or Grossräume, dominated by regional hegemons. Schmitt believed that the respective hegemons of the Grossräume should dominate coercively if necessary. But he also expected that such an order would be stable because, unlike universalist ideologies, it accepted the coexistence of different political systems.
The Schmittian focus on stability and coexistence resonates with the New Right’s opposition to forever wars and rejection of universalist schemes. The relative restraint of civilizationism also distinguishes the New Right from both the crusading neoconservativism that often invoked the defense of Western civilization to justify military interventions and the Huntingtonian prediction that civilizations will clash. Civilizationism is thus best defined as a hierarchical and antiuniversalist grand strategy that views regional imperialism as the most legitimate and most promising way to order the world. In practice, the strategy asserts that the United States ought to seek dominance over the Western Hemisphere, interfere in Europe’s affairs to support far-right forces that share a civilizationist worldview, and both disengage from and respect other civilizations’ spheres of influence.
Civilizationism differs markedly from Trump’s approach to the world. Although the Trump administration often speaks the language of civilizationism, Trump’s behavior is primarily motivated by personal grievance, transactional impulses, and a private interest in maximizing the wealth of his kin and clique. The biggest rupture between the administration’s foreign policy and civilizationism lies in Middle East policy. Contrary to his campaign promises, Trump did not retrench from the region, instead launching what he initially billed as a regime-change war against Iran. His attitude toward Israel—mostly treating it as a privileged ally—resembles that of neoconservative hawks such as the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham.
The American New Right is much less interested in championing Israel. The spread of a conspiratorial form of anti-Semitism in right-wing ranks is one driving factor, as is the decreasing popularity among American conservatives of a Christian Zionism that sees Israel as the fulfillment of biblical prophecies and, thus, the essential civilizational ally. But another explanation is strategic: many in the New Right believe the United States’ alliance with Israel traps Washington in a region where it has fought unnecessary and colossally costly wars. The scale of violence that Israel’s campaign in Gaza has inflicted has also contributed to a retreat from support, especially among younger conservatives.
Civilizationism also prescribes a different approach to China from the one Trump has taken. The second Trump administration has oscillated ambivalently between belligerently treating China as a dangerous rival and retrenching from East Asia. Supporters of the administration view this back and forth as a cunning ploy to buy time for the United States to position itself more advantageously for a confrontation. For others, the pivot to Asia is effectively dead. Either way, civilizationism would prescribe a more consistent strategy of military withdrawal from the region, a tack tantamount to tolerating Chinese hegemony in its sphere. In a coauthored 2022 New York Times essay, the prominent New Right commentators Sohrab Ahmari, Patrick Deneen, and Gladden Pappin, for example, have described China as a “civilizational equal” and called for pragmatic cooperation rather than “mindless China hawkism.” The New Right’s leading foreign policy thinker, Michael Anton, has explicitly stated that Taiwan is not worth fighting over.
Civilizationism has already had a strong influence on Trump’s foreign policy toward the Western Hemisphere and Europe. In a civilizationist understanding, a regional hegemon should assert its dominance over its backyard to provide order and exclude external powers. Controlling the Western Hemisphere is a particularly acute concern for the New Right, because migration from allegedly alien cultures and the inflow of drugs undermine the desired societal homogeneity and stability. Civilizationists see Europe as both the historic cradle of Western civilization and the key source of its greatest threat, liberalism. Aggressive interference in European affairs to prevent what Kevin Roberts, the Heritage Foundation’s president, has called “civilizational suicide” is thus justified almost as a form of domestic politics. Civilizationism would, however, intensify the Trump administration’s often haphazard and symbolic approach to undermining liberal EU governments and ultimately culturally vassalize Europe.
A civilizational grand strategy would not treat Russia as a threat and, thus, not sustain the U.S. security commitment to Europe. Some in the New Right stress civilizational affinities with Russia and argue for deeper bilateral relations, given that the country is anti-woke—or, according to Carlson, a “Christian country” that the United States has “a lot in common with.” Others advocate a pragmatic accommodation with Moscow that would grant it a sphere of influence over eastern Europe.
If Washington were to adopt a consistent civilizational grand strategy, it would completely upend U.S. foreign policy. It would allow for previously unthinkable concessions to the United States’ geopolitical rivals. Civilizationism would pose a historic challenge to the already battered transatlantic relationship by granting Russia de facto control over eastern Europe or treating Moscow as part of a common Western civilization and agitating more openly against sitting governments in Europe. Other historical U.S. alliances would suffer, too. Tolerating Chinese regional hegemony would throw East Asian allies under the bus, and disengaging from the Middle East would leave Israel to fend for itself.
But civilizationism is riddled with contradictions that would quickly become apparent if it ever did become Washington’s guiding policy. As the scholar Amitav Acharya has written, civilizations are “myths in the analytical sense.” Over time, no existing civilization has remained ethnically or culturally pure or set in the same borders. Indeed, civilizations are not so easily delineated: Where would a Russian civilization end? Should it include Georgia, the Baltic states, or Finland? How far does the United States’ civilizational sphere reach into Latin America?
It is also unlikely that a civilizational order would be peaceful. Civilizational claims could overlap and become a recipe for regional wars. By defining other civilizations as alien cultures, a civilizationist grand strategy might fuel antagonism rather than tolerate differences. Even European far-right parties seem increasingly uninterested in being so overtly backed by their U.S. counterparts. And even if great-power conflict could be avoided, intracivilizational violence would abound. Japan, Pakistan, and Poland would be unlikely to accept regional hegemony by China, India, or Russia, respectively.
The New Right is also not a unitary camp. National conservatives, for instance, oppose loosening the United States’ ties with Israel and tolerating Chinese and Russian imperialism. Others are still in favor of a crusade against the civilizational enemies China and Iran. Moreover, the New Right’s overriding focus has remained on domestic policy, with foreign policy often an afterthought.
But the American right wing’s ideological future, and the future of U.S. grand strategy, is wide open. The Trump administration has broken with the bipartisan post–Cold War consensus on liberal hegemony but has failed to offer a coherent alternative. In the coming contest to define Washington’s foreign policy, civilizationism is poised to be a central contender.
articles.summary: Civilizationism would upend America’s role in the world.

articles.title: Maximum Pressure on Iran Will Fail
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
NATE SWANSON is a Resident Senior Fellow and Director of the Iran Strategy Project at the Atlantic Council. He served as Director for Iran at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2025. In the spring and summer of 2025, he served on the Trump administration’s Iran negotiating team.
For 47 years, the Islamic Republic has bedeviled U.S. presidents. The 1979 Iran hostage crisis helped doom Jimmy Carter’s reelection bid. The Iran-contra scandal in the mid-1980s badly tarnished Ronald Reagan’s foreign policy record. And Barack Obama’s 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), led to an unprecedented situation in which the U.S. Congress invited a foreign leader, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to Washington to argue against it.
In February, when he launched his war against Iran, President Donald Trump declared that he intended to break this embarrassing pattern once and for all. By crushing Iran militarily and effecting regime change, he boasted that whereas other presidents had only talked about the Iranian threat, he was taking decisive action to end it. But six months later, Trump has become yet another U.S. president facing a dangerous humiliation related to Iran; the fallout from his excursion threatens his party’s prospects in the midterm elections. Now, perhaps in desperation, Trump is attempting to squeeze Tehran with an economic noose. But as it is constructed, this economic-pressure operation poses a greater threat to U.S. credibility than it does to Iran’s economy.
In truth, the multifaceted war Trump has launched is not a break with precedent but the apotheosis of the same flawed strategy that has undergirded U.S. policy toward Iran from the Islamic Republic’s inception, in 1979. Iran’s theocratic regime has continually flummoxed U.S. administrations in part because it contains profound contradictions. It is simultaneously ideological and transactional. Tehran continues to adhere to the core features of its revolutionary ideology, including its anti-American and anti-Israeli foreign policy, but can also act with pragmatism when circumstances demand it. Iran accepted meaningful limits on its nuclear program in 2015, for instance, and reversed decades of hostility toward Saudi Arabia by normalizing ties in 2023. Iran’s relationship to the U.S. national interest is confusing, too. The regime does pose a direct threat to the United States because of its illicit nuclear program. And long before the current war began, the terrorism and proxy militias Iran funded were menacing U.S. citizens and shipping through the Red Sea. Yet for most Americans, Iran remains a distant afterthought. A war that has extensively destroyed Iranian infrastructure, distorted the country’s economy, and killed an entire echelon of leaders, as well as thousands of soldiers and civilians, has had almost no impact on the United States other than driving up gas prices.
To address these dualities, Washington has often stripped nuance from policymaking and oriented U.S. strategy around pressure as the primary tool to contain Iran and compel it to behave differently. This pressure strategy has rested on two pillars: establishing a credible military threat and engaging in economic coercion. But instead of resolving the perplexing paradoxes posed by the Islamic Republic, this approach only deepened them—especially as Trump has sought to intensify the pressure strategy. A wave of domestic protests in January showed that Iran is internally combustible, but the war proved that the Islamic Republic is resilient and will not capitulate. Airstrikes have weakened the regime militarily but strengthened its standing internally. Iran acknowledges that it needs sanctions relief, but it is also learning that time is on its side and that, by controlling the Strait of Hormuz, it can impose reciprocal consequences for pressure.
The irony of Trump’s failed war on Iran—and his stop-start negotiations to try to end it—is that it has so severely weakened Washington’s ability to exert pressure on Tehran that no future administration will ever be able to revert to the traditional U.S. playbook. But that could also be the only upside of a war that has already exacted a heavy toll on U.S. munitions and the global economy. The war could—and should—force a broader reckoning with 47 years of failed strategy and change Washington’s approach for good.
In 2006, former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger wrote in The Washington Post that Iran’s leaders must “decide whether they are representing a nation or a cause.” He argued that Iran must choose between prioritizing stability and the well-being of its people—by engaging rationally with other states—or continuing to be driven by the revolutionary and ideological ambitions that defined the 1979 Iranian Revolution. This idea reflected U.S. policy toward Iran over the better part of 50 years. Washington wants Iran to abandon its revolutionary origins and aimed U.S. policy toward compelling that outcome. It has continually attempted to contain Iran’s influence and get Tehran to behave rationally using a mix of a few carrots and a lot of sticks; the biggest stick was the threat of a U.S. invasion.
Tehran itself has not seen a need to make such a concrete choice. The Islamic Republic has alternately—or simultaneously—behaved like a cause and a rational nation. For all its public bravado, the Iranian regime long sought to avoid direct conflict with the United States. The Islamic Republic’s first supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, famously asserted that Tehran was not afraid of the American military, but both he and his successor, Ali Khamenei, governed as if they were. In 1988, for instance, Khomeini finally agreed to end his war with Iraq after the United States began engaging Iranian naval ships in direct skirmishes, leading him to fear that Reagan might formally align with Saddam Hussein’s regime. Likewise, after the United States invaded Iraq in 2003, Iran—fearing that it might be next—sought various de-escalation options with George W. Bush’s administration, including halting its nuclear weapons program and sending emissaries to the State Department and the White House to explore détente.
When I served on the Trump administration’s Iran negotiating team in the first half of 2025, I was surprised to find that Iranian negotiators were focused less on gaining sanctions relief than on securing nonaggression pledges from the United States and Israel. An aversion to outright war with the United States is part of the reason Iran developed its network of proxy militias. It knew it could not win a direct conflict and so it pursued advantages elsewhere.
But this year’s war has taught the regime three new lessons. It has learned that it can survive massive U.S. and Israeli airstrikes that annihilate its leaders and inflict significant damage to its military and civilian infrastructure. Despite all that, its drone and missile capabilities remain intact enough to allow it to retaliate and stop maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has also discovered that the United States has no appetite for sending ground troops into its territory. Early in this year’s war, the United States and Israel considered launching ground operations to extract nuclear material but never initiated them, judging them to be highly risky and unlikely to affect the regime’s decision-making. This year’s war showed that regime change cannot be accomplished in Iran without a ground invasion, but even the most hawkish U.S. policymakers have not publicly recommended one—showing Tehran that Washington, in fact, has a limited ability to vanquish it militarily.
Finally, Iran gambled that it could outlast the United States in a conflict of attrition, and this bet has so far proved wise. The Iranian regime is willing to subject its own people to more suffering and economic pain than the U.S. public is willing to bear, especially since Americans broadly view the war as optional and, increasingly, as a quagmire. At multiple points, Trump has threatened to escalate, only to back down when energy prices spike. The threat of military force is now no longer as valuable as it was before the war—which is why Trump’s repeated military threats since the first cease-fire, in April, have not substantially changed Tehran’s actions.
The second historic bedrock of the United States’ pressure strategy has been economic coercion. Some sanctions, such as those designed to restrict Tehran’s ability to sell oil, have had a profound impact on Iran’s economy. But they have mostly failed to effect the policy changes they were designed to drive. Following the 1979 seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran—and Khomeini’s embrace of the takeover—Carter imposed a series of punitive actions, including an embargo on U.S. investment and trade with Iran. That move ended the two countries’ previously deep trade and defense partnership, but it did little to curtail Iran’s exports to the rest of the world. In 1996, Congress expanded the economic-pressure approach with the Iran Sanctions Act, which limited even non-Americans’ ability to invest in Iran’s energy sector. In 2012, Congress, as well as the European Union, further targeted Iran’s oil revenue and its central bank, cutting Iran’s oil exports in half virtually overnight. Those provisions were relaxed under the JCPOA, then reimposed in 2018 by the United States after Trump withdrew from the agreement and by Europe in 2025 when a so-called snapback clause triggered.
The first Trump administration’s “maximum pressure” strategy was initially advertised as a mechanism to secure a better nuclear deal. Once that failed to materialize, sanctioning Iran became an end in itself. More than 3,000 U.S. sanctions designations now target virtually every aspect of Iran’s government and economy. These sanctions are intentionally complex and layered with overlapping authorities, making them difficult to lift. But many are also symbolic. Over time, economic pressure—sanctions in particular—became an easy default policy for the U.S. government, even if many moves had no tangible impact, because they appeared to show Washington was taking action and Americans rarely bore any direct cost.
In the current war, Trump has cranked up economic pressure to its zenith by blockading Iranian ports. The war, however, finally imposed consequences on the American public when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz and targeted Gulf energy infrastructure, wreaking havoc on global energy shipments. Iran’s economy was already under tremendous strain before the war, and the blockade has exacerbated that strain. But Trump abandoned the first blockade after 66 days. He has recently imposed a second blockade and a broader pressure campaign aimed at curtailing Iran’s remaining trade that he advertises on social media as the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.” There is no doubt this campaign will hurt Iran and its economy. But it will almost certainly fail to force Tehran’s surrender. Rather than succumb to pressure, recent history suggests that Iran will use its missile and drone program to exact steep economic costs on the global economy—either in the Strait of Hormuz or against Gulf countries—to again shift Trump’s risk calculus. The Islamic Republic believes it can outlast the United States’ will to exert economic pressure, just as it can survive U.S. military pressure.
The failed war and blockades, as well as Trump’s approach to negotiations this year, will permanently alter the utility of economic pressure. Whereas sanctions relief was once the reward the United States could offer Iran for constraining its nuclear ambitions, Trump issued oil-export waivers in March without any Iranian concessions and again in June in return for a vow merely to keep the Strait of Hormuz open.
No matter how this war ends, the United States will not be able to return to the strategy that governed its relations with Iran for 47 years. Trump’s potential Republican successors, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, differ strikingly in their views of what to do next. In recent public comments, Rubio has suggested a preference for expanding a pressure strategy, telling Fox News in early August that the Iranian regime “must change” fundamentally and arguing that the United States should further ratchet up “the price” of intransigence A pressure strategy, however, was only sustainable, if not efficacious, insofar as it did not demand much from the American people. And with its newfound control of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran has far more ability to make the United States and its key Middle Eastern allies pay for applying pressure. Vance, by contrast, appears to favor retrenching from Iran and the Middle East more broadly—an approach that would loosely resemble Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s approach to Afghanistan, which cut the United States’ losses entirely. But Iran is a harder country to walk away from. Its nuclear program and strategic location give it direct leverage over the United States and the global economy in a way Afghanistan never did.
It is too early to know what path a Democratic administration would take, and there are no easy answers for how to approach Iran. There will be justified calls for diplomacy to take a more prominent role in U.S. policy. Like pressure, however, diplomacy cannot serve as an end in itself. A new approach must recognize the Islamic Republic’s persistent dualities, as well as the United States’ changing role in the Middle East. Over 20 years, a substantial U.S. presence in the region has not brought stability, and increasing that presence has not yielded better results. At the same time, the domestic grievances that led to the massive wave of January protests in Iran still exist. The United States might consider stepping back, forcing Iran’s leadership to focus more on governing and less on surviving a war. Instead of taking unilateral action, Washington should first seek the input and cooperation of allied capitals. And rather than try endlessly to build more leverage, it should instead better use what it has already accumulated.
The best thing Washington can do at this point is to stop acting without thinking. And U.S. policymakers need to dwell more on lessons from the past. Military and economic pressure did occasionally shape Iranian decision-making. Pressure helped push Iran to temporarily pause its nuclear program during George W. Bush’s administration and, later, to accept the JCPOA. But pressure did not topple the Islamic Republic, make the United States safer, or improve the lives of ordinary Iranians; in fact, the U.S. pressure strategy likely deepened Iranian civilians’ hardship.
Ultimately, what Washington wants most is for Iran to interact productively with its neighbors, abandon an illicit nuclear program, and promote the well-being of its people. But like it or not, the Islamic Republic gets a say in what happens next in Iran. Forty-seven years of prioritizing pressure culminated in a costly war that revealed the limits of what that approach can accomplish. It would be a silver lining if the Iran war’s failure forced a reckoning in Washington about the United States’ preconceived notions about Iran and the well-worn playbook that has led to this morass.
