articles.title: The End of Thailand’s Long Stalemate?
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
DUNCAN MCCARGO is President's Chair in Global Affairs at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
For more than 25 years, Thailand’s conservative establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle for the soul of the country. Royalists want palace institutions insulated from public criticism, a military licensed to intervene in times of political crisis, deferential political parties and politicians, and free rein to clamp down on political actors who fail to toe the line. The opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military that stays in the barracks, a competitive party system responsive to the people’s wishes, and predictable checks and balances that do not unduly punish elected politicians.
More often than not, the royalists have had the upper hand. They have mobilized protest movements, staged military coups, and banned opposition parties to prevent troublesome politicians from instituting changes that could limit their power and privileges. Yet every attempt to strike a decisive blow against the opposition has failed. Conservatives have not translated legal or extralegal victories into lasting governments. Opposition movements, meanwhile, have consistently reinvented themselves. Thaksin Shinawatra, the larger-than-life former policeman and telecom billionaire, built up enormous power as prime minister in the early 2000s, incurring the disdain of royalists. And even after a military coup removed Thaksin from the premiership in 2006, his parties remained electoral juggernauts. A yet more alarming challenge emerged on the horizon after a 2014 coup ousted Thaksin’s sister, Yingluck Shinawatra, from government: youth-based mass protests calling for reform of the monarchy in 2020 and progressive political parties who appealed to these younger voters.
A stalemate had prevailed over Thai politics, with neither side able to overpower the other fully. That changed in February 2026, when Bhumjaithai, a low-profile party previously known primarily for campaigning to legalize cannabis, swept into power in national elections. With the implicit backing of the monarchy and the conservative establishment, Bhumjaithai has seized control of the Thai state, giving rise to a new mode of politics capable of both suppressing progressive forces in favour of cozy collaboration among elites and winning a general election without overt manipulation.
Far from an electoral anomaly, the rise of Bhumjaithai is the culmination of a long effort by conservatives to retake the levers of power. In fact, the formerly also-ran party’s February triumph was part of a methodical, behind-the-scenes campaign to commandeer the state’s nominally neutral apparatuses, including its Senate and Constitutional Court. The alliance between the monarchical network and Bhumjaithai is more a marriage of convenience than a shared ideological project, and it may not last indefinitely. But shallow as it may be, it has already succeeded in decisively strengthening the conservative position, disempowering the major rival parties that threaten elite control, and potentially remaking the Thai state for years to come.
The origins of Thailand’s current political order date back to 1997, when a group of elite liberal royalists, claiming a mandate from civil society, introduced a landmark new charter. Often referred to as “the people’s constitution,” it was a reaction to a disastrous military coup in 1991 and its bloody aftermath, including the deadly suppression of unarmed protesters in May 1992. The reforms aimed to coup-proof the political system by introducing checks and balances to prevent elected politicians from abusing their power and facilitate a smooth royal succession. It established an electoral commission, a constitutional court, an anticorruption agency, and a human rights commission, as well as a fully elected, purportedly nonpartisan Senate.
The project backfired. It failed to stabilize Thai politics—probably an unrealistic goal to begin with—and the new parliamentary system allowed for the election of Thaksin as prime minister in 2001. A charismatic figure with populist authoritarian tendencies, he successfully mobilized lower-income voters in the heavily populated north and northeast regions of Thailand, melding them into an unbeatable electoral bloc. He used his considerable personal wealth, his party’s parliamentary dominance, and his bureaucratic connections to create a startlingly successful political machine. Thaksin bought off the Senate and the independent agencies, defanging them as neutral bodies, and installed loyalists in crucial posts intended to check the prime minister’s power.
The country’s traditional elites were deeply threatened by Thaksin’s ascendance. The so-called Yellow Shirt movement, which appropriated a royal color, sought to make Thailand ungovernable. Through mass street protests and the occupation of public spaces and buildings, it paralyzed opposition rule three times: in 2006, 2008, and in 2013–14. But for all its success in ousting opposition-led governments, the Yellow Shirt movement never solved a basic problem: conservatives could bring down an elected government, but they couldn’t win an election to replace it.
The 2006 and 2014 political crises initially followed a similar pattern. Street protests destabilized and delegitimized Shinawatra-led governments, and military coups then removed them. Each time, the establishment brought in the Royal Thai Army to reorganize politics, rewrite the constitution, and reconfigure the party system in its favor before holding fresh elections. But military force failed to bring about durable conservative rule. Coups were short-term fixes that gradually eroded the legitimacy of the establishment. The Thai public was willing to tolerate only short interludes of military rule, and coup makers had no choice but to promise the imminent restoration of democracy. Generals, however, were bad at politics. The public quickly tired of them, and voters soon welcomed back the same kinds of politicians that soldiers had kicked out. In the 2007 elections, the first called by the ruling junta after the 2006 coup, for instance, Thaksin’s party was voted back into power. The experience was imprinted on the minds of conservatives when they launched the 2014 coup; the new government postponed elections until 2019.
The inability of conservatives to break the opposition once and for all persuaded the establishment to try to cut deals with Thaksin’s Pheu Thai Party instead. A strategy of conciliation permitted the opposition to front a government as long as party leaders concentrated on managing the economy and did not challenge the special status of the monarchy. Pheu Thai, conservatives believed, could always be co-opted or browbeaten into a politics of benefit sharing in which wealth and power were divided between a Pheu Thai figurehead and conservative power brokers. This was the deal behind Yingluck Shinawatra’s administration of 2011 to 2014, an arrangement that both conservatives and Thaksin supporters found unsatisfying and were reluctant to acknowledge.
But government by veto was inherently unstable. Eventually, the conservatives were unable to tolerate ambitious, independent-minded Pheu Thai administrations and brought them crashing down, as they did in the 2014 military coup. Where they did not want to use force, they turned to lawfare to limit the opposition’s power. Starting in 2019, a series of more progressive “orange” opposition parties proved wildly popular, especially among younger voters. After the orange Move Forward Party won the largest number of seats in Thailand’s National Assembly in the 2023 elections, the military-appointed Senate blocked its leader, Pita Limjaroenrat, from assuming the premiership. The following year, Move Forward was summarily dissolved—the fifth major opposition party to meet this fate—and the Constitutional Court banned Pita from political office for ten years.
By 2025, the establishment was running out of options to disempower the opposition. Challenged by both pro-Thaksin forces and progressive orange parties, its old methods—military coups, dodgy deals, party bans, the judicial removal of prime ministers—were wearing thin. Conservatives desperately needed an alliance with a reliably deferential party that could win elections.
Enter Bhumjaithai, a previously medium-sized party based in the northeastern province of Buriram. The product of a breakaway by a faction of members of parliament and former ministers from Thaksin’s party in 2008, Bhumjaithai had for the first 17 years of its existence no popular politicians among its ranks, no clear economic policies, and no national following.
Yet under the guidance of the shadowy Newin Chidchob, Bhumjaithai has gradually become a force in Thai politics and a crucial ally of the monarchy and its sympathizers. Known euphemistically by the party faithful as “the school principal,” Newin served as a junior minister under Thaksin and in other governments but stepped back from frontline politics two decades ago, ostensibly to concentrate on building up his Buriram United soccer team. He neither grants interviews nor appears in public but exercises tight control over Bhumjaithai’s strategy and personnel. Current Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, a U.S.-trained engineer and former deputy minister whose family owns the massive Sino-Thai Engineering and Construction company, has served as the party’s leader and public face since 2012.
What Newin and Anutin lack in ideological vision, they have made up for in strategic cunning, accumulating power wherever possible and making themselves useful to the monarchical network. Correctly diagnosing the establishment’s desperate need for a reliable political party with which to collaborate, they set out to distinguish their party from other conservative contenders, which were typically packed with reliable but often underperforming former bureaucrats. To do so, Newin and Anutin transformed Bhumjaithai into a major vehicle for influential provincial business interests.
Control of the key ministries was a crucial first step in the project to capture state power. As a precondition to joining coalition governments as a junior partner, Bhumjaithai demanded ministerial positions that would help it secure stronger local networks. In 2019, Anutin became minister of public health and subsequently boosted the pay of over one million health volunteers in villages across the country. Anutin’s support turned many of them into canvassers for Bhumjaithai—an electoral masterstroke, given that Thai elections are often won and lost in these provincial areas, where vote-canvasser networks are all-important. Then, in 2023, Bhumjaithai secured control of the powerful Ministry of Interior, which oversees local governance in Thailand, including more than 70,000 village headmen. In the right hands, the Interior Ministry can be a formidable patronage machine, exerting authority over everything from local budgets to Senate elections. The party then combined the health and headmen networks to penetrate every community in Thailand. Today, Anutin still holds the post of interior minister, in addition to his position as prime minister.
Other behind-closed-doors moves solidified Bhumjaithai’s power. For most Thai citizens, the selection of 200 new senators in 2024 through an arcane and untested self-nomination system barely registered, creating ample opportunity for manipulation. Candidates linked to Bhumjaithai gamed the system and secured around two-thirds of the supposedly neutral upper chamber—a majority that has allowed conservative forces to quietly block independent-minded candidates for the Constitutional Court, the Election Commission, and the Anticorruption Commission and to exercise veto power over any future changes to the constitution.
Missteps by the opposition also smoothed the path for the party’s ultimate takeover of the state. When the Bhumjaithai-controlled Constitutional Court removed Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, as prime minister in August 2025, the orange party—now known as the People’s Party—voted for Anutin, rather than another Pheu Thai member, to replace her. People’s Party leaders naively believed a Bhumjaithai government would be in office for only a brief period and that after winning an early election, progressive forces could push to amend the constitution and reduce the entrenched power of the elite. This was a disastrous miscalculation. In the February election, Bhumjaithai shocked most observers by decisively topping the polls, winning 192 seats to the People’s Party’s 120 seats. With Bhumjaithai in control of both the internal levers of power and parliament, the prospects for progressive constitutional reform evaporated.
By neutralizing the Pheu Thai and the People’s Party, Bhumjaithai has made itself the most successful conservative party in modern Thai history. Far from transforming the country’s politics, however, this dominance has ground it to a halt. The incarnation of transactional conservatism, Bhumjaithai now controls every major mechanism of the state. But whereas in the past the various royalist and opposition factions jockeying for influence each stood for something tangible, the party is a cipher, favored by many conservatives, yet largely devoid of ideological or policy content or an organic base of support.
Today, a country known for mobilizing millions of people around big ideas, both during hotly contested elections and through massive extraparliamentary movements, is led by a party with no apparent ideas at all. The political reform project that began in the 1990s has run its course. So, too, have Thaksin’s project to empower the disadvantaged, the military’s nationalist project to restore order and defend the monarchy, and the progressive project to transform Thailand into a more open and equal place.
At the same time, Bhumjaithai’s vacuous opportunism reflects a new form of realpolitik that appears much more durable than previous iterations. Royalists have grudgingly rallied around the party because they have nowhere else to go. Thaksin, recently chastened by an eight-month prison term, has gone quiet. Progressives criticize and deconstruct what they decry as the “blue regime” (after the color of Bhumjaithai’s logo) but struggle to articulate a realistic strategy to challenge it. Despite the contradictions that underpin Anutin’s government, it has shown no sign of imminent collapse.
This hollow dominance has yielded a strange impasse. For the last six months, Anutin’s administration has mostly treaded water, postponing major initiatives. That impasse may not hold as younger generations become a force in Thai politics. Indeed, conservatives’ grip on power remains deeply contested and contingent. A united opposition that puts aside the long-standing differences between pro-Thaksin and progressive forces could in theory topple Bhumjaithai at the ballot box. A return to Move Forward’s winning slogan in 2023—a Thailand that is “not the same as before,” code for the dismantling of gerontocracy and unearned privilege across the country’s creaking structures and institutions—could serve as the basis for an alternative administration. But even if an anti-Bhumjaithai coalition were to take back power, it would struggle to unwind the party’s control of Thailand’s political institutions. However long Bhumjaithai’s present tenure in Bangkok lasts, that takeover of the levers of state power will be its enduring legacy.

articles.title: Why Criminals Love the Chinese Economy
articles.full_text:
Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.
ALVIN CAMBA is Lead Scientist and Director of Research at Lyvi and a Nonresident Fellow in the Indo-Pacific Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
For years, international discussion of China’s economic rise has focused on how it has built a manufacturing and export powerhouse and used industrial policy to support such efforts at a continental scale. But there is another, darker side of China’s dominance: its outsize role in the illicit global economy. China purchases roughly 90 percent of Iran’s sanctioned oil exports, which often arrive relabeled as originating from Malaysia and are paid for with money routed through small banks and shell companies acting as intermediaries. Cryptocurrency brokers in China and Hong Kong help North Korean hackers, such as the notorious Lazarus Group, convert stolen coins into usable cash. And China-based networks support money launderers working with Mexican cartels selling fentanyl, online scam centers in Southeast Asia, and the global wildlife trafficking trade.
Data from organizations and governments tracking illegal activity suggests that the Chinese illicit economy generates nearly $1 trillion in revenue annually, about the size of Switzerland’s GDP. Roughly two-thirds of counterfeit goods seized by customs authorities worldwide originate in China or move through Hong Kong, and the notorious scam compounds that have proliferated in Southeast Asia—many of which are operated by or linked to Chinese criminal networks—have trafficked more than 300,000 people from at least 66 countries into forced labor while generating roughly $40 billion in profits each year.
Beijing has tried to crack down on some of these activities. In the Philippines, China’s Ministry of Public Security canceled the passports of hundreds of Chinese nationals involved in offshore gambling operations there, turning them into fugitives who can be arrested and deported. Since 2023, joint operations between China and Myanmar have led to the arrest of more than 57,000 Chinese nationals suspected of telecom fraud, the closure of dozens of scam compounds along the China-Myanmar border, and the execution of several bosses running these compounds. The United States, too, wants to stop these activities: the Trump administration launched the Scam Center Strike Force to investigate fraud centers in Southeast Asia, and the president signed an executive order directing the government to prioritize cybercrime, including predatory schemes.
Yet none of these actions have significantly curtailed the illicit economy. If anything, it is growing larger. This is in part because these illegal activities are driven by many of the same forces that underpin China’s legal economy. Criminal groups have exploited the core financial and commercial infrastructure that developed in response to China’s strict capital controls and its industrial overcapacity. Beijing’s enforcement, although real, is selective and partial because elements of the illicit economy serve the country’s larger strategic goals, such as sustaining trade with Russia while maintaining distance from the war in Ukraine. What may appear to be a collection of unrelated crimes is intertwined with China’s imbalanced growth model and its foreign policy. As Washington struggles to compete with China, Beijing’s role in the global illicit economy is working against U.S. priorities around the world.
The central forces driving China’s illicit economy are the structural imbalances created by the country’s economic model. One of the most important is financial: strict capital controls have created enormous demand to move money out of China. China’s economic boom has produced fabulous wealth, including more than 800 billionaires. But Beijing restricts how this wealth can leave the country. China has a quota limiting individuals to purchasing $50,000 in foreign currency each year, and they cannot freely convert domestic currency to move wealth abroad. With deposits in China generating low returns and no access to more lucrative foreign assets to invest in, wealthy individuals and business owners have sought to find ways to funnel their money out of the country.
Starting in the 1990s, underground bankers set up shell companies and bank accounts in Hong Kong to circumvent mainland China’s capital controls. These companies and accounts, often disguised as trading firms, settled transactions involving renminbi collected inside China against dollars held offshore. In addition, brokers and financial intermediaries routed payments to offshore counterparties to allow Chinese citizens to use domestic currency to purchase property abroad or to trade overseas investment for foreign visas and passports. Meanwhile, junket operators, who brought wealthy clients to casinos in Macau, extended credit to them in Hong Kong dollars and then collected the debts in mainland China in renminbi. This allowed them to settle debts at home while picking up currency abroad, facilitating capital flight on a large scale.
The same underground banking networks built to move private Chinese wealth became useful to criminal groups that also needed to transfer money across borders and conceal its origins. Drug cartels, for instance, have used them to launder their proceeds. Financial intermediaries match drug traffickers seeking to get rid of extra dollars with Chinese clients seeking to obtain dollars abroad. Similar networks also have provided the financial channels that help Chinese suppliers evade Western sanctions while selling ingredients such as nitrocellulose, used to make munitions, to Russia, or sodium perchlorate, a precursor for missile propulsion, to Iran.
Financial intermediaries and criminal fraud enterprises are coming into closer proximity, which is making their activities harder to disentangle and disrupt. Political changes such as China’s anticorruption campaign pushed casino junket operators and underground financiers from their established bases in Hong Kong, Macau, and mainland China to Cambodia, the Philippines, and other locations in Southeast Asia. In these places, they converged with criminal networks that had established business and political relationships. Scam networks generate the proceeds, while underground financiers launder and move the money through many of the same channels Chinese clients use to move private wealth offshore. A 2023 anti-money-laundering operation in Singapore showed how financial channels and fraud networks have become deeply interwoven. Authorities seized condos, gold, cryptocurrency, and bank accounts eventually valued at more than $2.2 billion, and arrested ten people, all of whom were originally from China and most of whom held Cambodian, Cypriot, Turkish, or Vanuatuan passports. Singaporean police traced members of the network to overseas scams and illegal online gambling operations.
China’s industrial overcapacity has also lowered the costs of building and operating illicit enterprises. Starting in 2021, China’s real estate slowdown weakened domestic demand for steel, cement, and other construction materials. Excess construction materials exported from China, together with Chinese construction services, helped casinos, special economic zones, and scam compounds develop rapidly in Southeast Asia while supporting Chinese export revenues. The glut of products in China’s vast electronics industry, including cheap phones, computers, and communications equipment, made it economical for criminal networks to operate fraud at industrial scale. When Myanmar’s military raided Shwe Kokko, one of the country’s largest scam compounds, in November 2025, it seized nearly 10,000 mobile phones—most of which were likely made in China—from a single site. Overcapacity in China’s oil-refining sector, too, has made discounted Iranian crude particularly attractive to independent refiners.
Despite sporadic enforcement efforts, the benefits that leaders at different levels of the Chinese government accrue from the illicit economy make it difficult to stop. Local officials want to protect economically valuable firms and financial flows that keep their economies afloat, even if they are engaged in illegal activity, and Beijing selectively tolerates questionable flows of money and goods when they serve its strategic interests. Institutions connected to the Chinese Communist Party also play a role: some figures in organizations connected to the United Front, the party’s apparatus for building influence at home and abroad, as well as some members of overseas Chinese associations, overlap with criminal networks doing business overseas. This gives them networks of access to political elites in host countries while drawing them into pro-Beijing influence activities abroad.
Provincial governments, whose leaders face strong incentives to deliver growth, benefit from economic activity whether it is generated by legitimate business expansion or the illicit economy. In Fujian, for instance, officials in the city of Ningde backed the battery manufacturer CATL and built an industrial cluster around it to support industrial growth. In Anxi County, by contrast, local operators with fewer economic opportunities but access to informal financial channels set up a sprawling telecom-fraud network that eventually expanded into Southeast Asia. Ningde and Anxi were both embedded in Fujian’s broader networks of commerce, migration, and finance, but they had radically different outcomes: a globally competitive industrial cluster in one and an illicit transnational economy in the other. In both cases, leaders could point to high levels of economic growth.
Local support for illicit economic activity can also support Beijing’s foreign policy goals. In 2024, trade between Russia and the northeastern Chinese province of Heilongjiang reached $32.2 billion, part of a broader commercial relationship in which Chinese firms have supplied Russia with machine tools, microelectronics, and other dual-use goods that could be used for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Some of these sales go to entities facing U.S. sanctions. Although Beijing describes such trade as ordinary commerce, conducting it through provincial and private firms helps ensure that any potential sanctions fall on intermediaries rather than the party-state itself. And it is private brokers, shell companies, and financial intermediaries in Hong Kong and mainland China, not official state institutions, that clear Iranian oil purchases and North Korean cryptocurrency cash-outs, also giving Beijing distance from transactions that violate U.S. sanctions.
In a small number of cases, there may even be direct connections between crime bosses and Chinese intelligence agencies. Through their private business dealings, bosses can penetrate ruling parties in other countries and gain proximity to political leaders and access to information that China’s official embassies cannot easily obtain. In one prominent example, She Zhijiang, a crime boss responsible for developing the Shwe Kokko scam center in Myanmar, claimed while fighting extradition in Bangkok that he heeded instructions from China’s Ministry of State Security. He also alleged that a mayor of a small municipality in the Philippines, who local authorities determined was a Chinese national, was a Chinese state asset. The Philippines sentenced her to life imprisonment for human trafficking connected to her role in running an online gambling operation.
In certain circumstances, Beijing is willing to crack down on illegal activity. When Chinese citizens are victims of kidnapping or fraud, as was the case in the scam centers along the Myanmar border, Chinese authorities move quickly and make arrests. Likewise, when crime bosses become international liabilities that could hamper Beijing’s relations with other countries, or when their political patrons fall and there are fewer political costs to targeting them, Beijing will act. In October 2025, for example, the United States indicted Chen Zhi, the Chinese-born mastermind behind Prince Group, one of Southeast Asia’s largest criminal conglomerates. After many countries froze or seized assets linked to him, China called for his arrest and requested his extradition from Cambodia. Trying criminal leaders such as Chen in China is an ideal outcome for Beijing: it demonstrates to foreign audiences that China is enforcing the law, while also reducing the risk that testimony about state links could emerge in foreign courtrooms.
Where possible, Beijing and Washington should work together to fight back against illegal activity. China does not want underground banking networks allowing capital to flee the country. Beijing’s Sky Net repatriation operations, which since 2015 have pursued and returned thousands of corrupt officials and economic fugitives to China, are an explicit acknowledgment that infrastructure to move money abroad and conceal overseas assets hinders Chinese state control. As the United States and China continue high-level talks, constraining the underground financial architecture of the illicit economy is an opportunity for a mutual diplomatic win. They could start by exchanging information on shell companies identified by their respective financial intelligence units and by coordinating crackdowns on the largest underground banking networks. Such an arrangement would echo the two countries’ collaboration in setting up a counternarcotics working group, in January 2024, to fight fentanyl trafficking.
But in other areas in which Beijing is not ready or willing to address the problem, Washington should use its own tools. Washington can institutionalize cooperation among states with shared interests in fighting transnational crime linked to Southeast Asia—Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, and Thailand—through a standing arrangement for sharing information about transactions tied to identified China-linked illicit finance networks. Working together to track these flows would reduce the chance that international criminals can extend their reach beyond any single jurisdiction. The Financial Action Task Force, an intergovernmental body, has established standards for combating cross-border money laundering; what is missing is a political commitment among U.S. allies and partners to systematically share operational data on China-linked illicit finance networks. Governments could draw on data collected by the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and allied financial intelligence units to identify transactions tied to these networks. A standing arrangement would turn that commitment into routine practice.
The U.S. Treasury Department can also invoke Section 311 of the U.S.A. Patriot Act, which authorizes the Treasury secretary to designate a foreign financial institution as “of primary money laundering concern” and cut it off from accounts in the United States. Washington can apply this to Chinese and Hong Kong financial institutions that facilitate purchases of Iranian oil, launder cartel proceeds, or convert stolen cryptocurrency into usable funds. Treasury has shown it is willing to use this authority. In 2017, it employed Section 311 against a Chinese bank for serving as a financial conduit for North Korea, and in October 2025, it issued a final rule severing Cambodia’s Huione Group from the U.S. financial system because of its role in laundering money connected to North Korean cyber-heists and Southeast Asian scam centers. Similar actions could impose costs on the financial institutions handling tens of billions of dollars in revenues from sanctioned Iranian oil each year.
For too long, the United States has let illicit activity slide even though much of it undercuts U.S. foreign policy priorities. Washington has failed to stop Chinese purchases of Iranian oil despite U.S. sanctions, hollowing out efforts to limit money reaching the Islamic Republic. Cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean hackers and laundered through Chinese financial intermediaries provides funds for Pyongyang’s weapons programs, undermining international nonproliferation policy. The scam compounds that Chinese networks have built across Southeast Asia now take tens of billions of dollars a year from victims worldwide, including from people in the United States. China’s structural imbalances are fueling this illegal economic activity. If the United States really wants to compete with China and push back against the consequences of its economic rise, it will have to deal with what’s on the books as well as what’s not.
